result:
We never meet ourselves. Not really. The person in the mirror is a left-right flip of the real thing — a stranger with our hair parting on the wrong side, our smile curving in reverse. Photographs betray us differently. They catch us mid-blink, mid-thought, frozen in an expression we never felt ourselves make. Video is closer, maybe, but even then we flinch. Who is that person talking with their hands, laughing too loud, leaning in?

I think about this on buses, watching people. Every face I see is a face its owner has never truly seen. The woman by the window with the chipped nail polish and the paperback — she knows herself from the inside, from the fog of thought and the pull of mood. I know her only as a silhouette against the glass, a study in concentration. There is something almost tender in it: all these private worlds, traveling together.

We are unreadable to ourselves and legible, in some small way, to strangers. Maybe that's why we love old home videos, why we mourn the unrecorded. We're hoping, in some dim way, to catch a glimpse of the self everyone else has been talking to all along — the self that exists out in the world, in the light, in the company of others.

The mirror is a practical tool and a small tragedy. It shows us just enough to get dressed, to fix our hair, to confirm, each morning, that we're still here. It never shows us who arrived.
